ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study was approved by the Bath Spa Ethics Committee (ref: 010724NC).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of six groups (see Figure 1) in an experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: combined label [HWLs & calorie labelling] vs HWL only vs calorie labelling only) x 2 (Message Type: description vs description + example image) factorial design.
table.formatted: Participants were randomly assigned to one of six groups (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>) in an experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: combined label [HWLs & calorie labelling] vs HWL only vs calorie labelling only) x 2 (Message Type: description vs description + example image) factorial design.

table.text: Eligible participants were adults (18+, the legal minimum age for alcohol use in the United Kingdom), residing in the UK.
Participants were recruited to the study via Prolific, which has a pool of over 150,000 participants (https://www.prolific.com/).
table.formatted: Participants were recruited to the study via Prolific, which has a pool of over 150,000 participants (<ref type="url" target="https://www.prolific.com/">https://www.prolific.com/</ref>).

table.text: The sample was nationally representative based on Prolific quotas (for age, gender, and ethnicity).
Participants were unaware of their group assignment throughout the study.

In the description only condition, participants were told that the study was aiming to elicit opinions on a potential policy that the government could implement and were then presented with a description of the policy.
In the description plus image conditions, participants were given the same information but were also presented with an example image of the intervention (see Figure 1).
table.formatted: In the description plus image conditions, participants were given the same information but were also presented with an example image of the intervention (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

table.text: Participants were first asked: 'Do you support or oppose a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products?', with responses on a seven-point scale from 1 (strongly oppose) to 7 (strongly support).

Participants were asked 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could make you feel motivated to drink less alcohol?' and 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could make others feel motivated to drink less alcohol?'.
table.header: Perceived effectiveness of the labelling policy

table.text: Participants were asked 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could lead to harms to you?' and 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could lead to harms for the public?'.
table.header: Perceived unintended consequences of the labelling policy

table.text: To ensure that participants were paying attention to the questions and reading them properly, after the primary outcome participants were asked 'Please select the response 'strongly agree'' from a set of options.

Participants were asked open-ended questions where they could provide their thoughts on the government labelling policy, particularly in relation to acceptability, perceived effectiveness and potential adverse effects, as well as any further comments.

After reading the information sheet and consenting to take part, participants completed screening questions relating to their typical consumption of alcohol and indicated their preferred beverage (either beer or wine) to determine which drink type they viewed in the image conditions.
If no preference was indicated, they were randomised to view either beer or wine.
Participants were then asked questions regarding their demographic characteristics.
Participants were randomised to one of six groups (see 'Intervention' section).
Following completion, participants were debriefed, including receiving information about the study and the health consequences of consuming excess alcohol.
Participants were reimbursed for their time via Prolific.
Inattentive participants were screened out via the embedded attention check.

Figure 2 shows the flow of participants through the study and Table 1 the demographic characteristics by group. 1014 participants were recruited into the study; 7 of these dropped out, 9 failed attention checks and 4 were identified as potential bots using bot detection within Qualtrics.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: There was no direct evidence available within the literature from which to estimate the effect of these different label formats on acceptability. A maximum sample size of 1000 was possible with available resources (~166/per group). With 80% power and at alpha 5%, 1000 participants would detect Cohen's d of 0.2 or greater between the six groups with a 2-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 44 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants were randomly assigned to one of six groups (see Figure 1) in an experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: combined label [HWLs & calorie labelling] vs HWL only vs calorie labelling only) x 2 (Message Type: description vs description + example image) factorial design.
Eligible participants were adults (18+, the legal minimum age for alcohol use in the United Kingdom), residing in the UK.
Participants were recruited to the study via Prolific, which has a pool of over 150,000 participants (https://www.prolific.com/).
The sample was nationally representative based on Prolific quotas (for age, gender, and ethnicity).
Participants were unaware of their group assignment throughout the study.

In the description only condition, participants were told that the study was aiming to elicit opinions on a potential policy that the government could implement and were then presented with a description of the policy.
In the description plus image conditions, participants were given the same information but were also presented with an example image of the intervention (see Figure 1).

Participants were first asked: 'Do you support or oppose a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products?', with responses on a seven-point scale from 1 (strongly oppose) to 7 (strongly support).

Participants were asked 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could make you feel motivated to drink less alcohol?' and 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could make others feel motivated to drink less alcohol?'.

Participants were asked 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could lead to harms to you?' and 'Do you think a government policy of putting this label on alcohol products could lead to harms for the public?'.

To ensure that participants were paying attention to the questions and reading them properly, after the primary outcome participants were asked 'Please select the response 'strongly agree'' from a set of options.

Participants were asked open-ended questions where they could provide their thoughts on the government labelling policy, particularly in relation to acceptability, perceived effectiveness and potential adverse effects, as well as any further comments.

After reading the information sheet and consenting to take part, participants completed screening questions relating to their typical consumption of alcohol and indicated their preferred beverage (either beer or wine) to determine which drink type they viewed in the image conditions.
If no preference was indicated, they were randomised to view either beer or wine.
Participants were then asked questions regarding their demographic characteristics.
Participants were randomised to one of six groups (see 'Intervention' section).
Following completion, participants were debriefed, including receiving information about the study and the health consequences of consuming excess alcohol.
Participants were reimbursed for their time via Prolific.
Inattentive participants were screened out via the embedded attention check.

Figure 2 shows the flow of participants through the study and Table 1 the demographic characteristics by group. 1014 participants were recruited into the study; 7 of these dropped out, 9 failed attention checks and 4 were identified as potential bots using bot detection within Qualtrics.

Finally, the sample was representative of the UK population but participants were highly educated overall, although there is evidence to suggest that responses to labelling may not differ by SES group (Robinson et al., 2022).

text.text: Improved alcohol labels are a population-level intervention with the potential to reduce selection and consumption of alcohol.

The primary aim of this study was to assess the acceptability of implementing (i) alcohol calorie labelling, (ii) alcohol health warning labels (HWLs), and (iii) both types of labels combined, each presented with or without images.
The specific labels used were based on those being proposed for national implementation in Ireland.

Participants (n=994) were randomly assigned to one of six groups in an online experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: HWL only; calorie labelling only; combined label [HWLs and calorie labelling]) x 2 (Message Type: description; description plus example image) factorial design.
The primary outcome was acceptability of implementing the labelling policy.
Secondary outcomes were perceived effectiveness and potential harms.
Free-text comments were analysed using content analysis.
There was a significant main effect of Label Type (F(2, 990)=4.27, p=0.014, η²=0.01), with ₚ acceptability lower for HWLs (p=0.01, d=0.23).
There was no main effect of Message Type or interaction.
All types of labels were perceived as relatively acceptable.
There were no overall differences in perceived effectiveness or harms of the labels.
HWLs and calorie information were both perceived as relatively acceptable, although HWLs were less accepted.
The way the labelling policy was presented did not affect acceptability.

Although further evaluation with other labelling interventions is warranted, this suggests giving the public more detailed and visual information about a labelling policy does not decrease acceptability of the policy.
In an online randomised experiment, 994 participants viewed alcohol calorie labelling, alcohol health warning labels (HWLs), or both types of labels combined, either presented with or without images.
HWLs and calorie information were both perceived as relatively acceptable.
The way the labelling policy was presented did not affect acceptability.

text.text: These differences could in part be due to the way the policy is described or presented.

For example, in a study that described the policy (Reynolds et al., 2019) there was higher support for graphic HWLs (78% of participants supporting) compared to a study that showed participants an image of the label (34% supporting) (Clarke et al., 2020).

text.text: This may indicate that although the public do not oppose the concept of labelling, viewing the HWL may reduce support for them because they are designed to evoke negative emotions.

Exploring differences in the way a policy is presented to participants can inform researchers and policymakers as to how best to describe and present these types of policies to the public, including when assessing their potential support.

text.text: There was no evidence for a main effect of Message Type [F(1, 988) = 0.63, p = 0.43] or an interaction between Label Type and Message Type F(2, 988) = 1.37, p = 0.25].
In general, the labels were all relatively accepted by participants.

For all groups the proportion of participants that agreed to some extent with the labelling policies (indicated by a score of above 4) ranged from 77.8% (in the HWL only + image group) to 86% (in the calorie labelling only + image group).

There was no evidence of an effect of Label Type or Message Type on perceived effectiveness of the labels at changing the participant's behaviour or the public's behaviour [Label Type: F(2, 990) = 0.28, p = 0.757; Message Type: F(1, 990) = 2.12, p = 0.14].

In general, most participants indicated they did not feel the labels would be effective in getting them to drink less (scores above 4 indicating that they agreed to some extent with the statement), with the proportion ranging from 36% to 44%.
The proportions were higher for those who thought the labels might be effective in getting others to drink less, with proportions ranging from 59% to 65%.

There was no evidence for main effects of Label Type or Message Type on perceived potential harms to the participant or to the public [Label Type: F(2, 990) = 0.85, p = 0.427; Message Type: F(1, 990) = 0.005, p = 0.946].
There was evidence for a significant interaction for perceived harms to self [F (2, 988) = 3.87, p = 0.021, η² = 0.01].

Post-hoc comparisons ₚ (see supplementary material 2, Tables S4 and S5) indicated a significant difference between the calorie labelling only + image group and the combined label + image group (p = 0.03), with higher scores for the combined label (indicating higher perceived harms).

Post-hoc comparisons indicated a significant difference between ₚ description of the calorie labelling only group (with no image) and the description of the combined label group (with no image) (p = 0.016), with lower scores for the calorie label (indicating higher perceived harms to others).

In general, the proportion of participants that perceived harms to either themselves or to others for any of the label types (indicated by scores over 4) was low, with the proportion below 10% for both secondary outcomes in all groups.

As the overall analysis includes a label that combines both elements of the calorie and HWL label within the combined label, we conducted an analysis that included only the calorie and HWL labels in a 2 (Label Type: calorie vs HWL) x 2 (Message Type: description + image vs description only) ANOVA.
The results were similar to the primary outcome analysis.
There was a main effect of Label Type [F(1, 661) = 8.87, p = 0.003, η² = 0.01] and no evidence for ₚ a main effect of Message Type or interaction between Label Type and Message Type.
Overall, 988 participants left a free-text comment in response to at least one question.

Support for all labels was relatively high, with 40% (n=394) of participants leaving a comment that suggested they found the labels acceptable, 25% (n=249) of participants implying that they supported their implementation in some form, and only 7% (n=73) of participants leaving a comment that explicitly opposed the labels.

Overall, just over 50% (n=507) of participants emphasised that they thought the labels could reduce general drinking behaviour or have wider public health benefits, 17% (n=166) of participants highlighted they could lead to reductions in drinking for specific groups of people (e.g., heavier drinkers), and 32% (n=313) of participants thought they would not have any impact on drinking behaviour.
In terms of other potential benefits, 49% (n=486) emphasised that the labels could be useful for increasing knowledge and awareness (i.e., of health risks and calorie content).
Overall, 12% (n=116) of participants highlighted there may be potential for unintended harms either in general or for specific groups.

text.text: Overall, adding health warnings that describe the risk of liver disease and cancer to alcoholic products were less acceptable than adding calorie information, albeit both label types were relatively acceptable.

There was no evidence that there were any differences in acceptability, perceived effectiveness or potential for harms, between describing a labelling policy only versus describing with an accompanying image of the label.

The finding that health warnings are less acceptable than calorie labels is in line with other studies that compare support for these labelling policies (Clarke et al., 2023; Grummon et al., 2025), although -based on both the label ratings and the free text comments -all of the labels in the current study were relatively acceptable overall.

text.text: Despite this, future work should focus on how to increase the acceptability of HWLs, given their proposed implementation in many countries and continued policy interest (WHO, 2025).

text.text: Although there was a difference in acceptability between HWLs and calorie labels, there was no evidence of a difference in acceptability between these labels and the label that combined HWLs and calories.
More specifically, adding a HWL to calorie information does not seem to reduce acceptability.

Given many countries have implemented alcohol labels that contain multiple components (Kokole et al., 2026), this suggests labelling policies that combine multiple label types may be as acceptable to the public as the single label components.

text.text: Current findings therefore suggest the acceptability of this labelling policy is similar irrespective of whether it is described in text form or with an accompanying image and these earlier findings may be attributable to different samples and methods rather than an effect of describing vs visualising.

Many policy communications occur through different modalities that often use imagery, such as print, broadcast, and social media, with social media shown to be the most widely used globally (Mede et al., 2025).

text.text: Current findings suggest that a visual policy instrument such as labels is unaffected by mode of communication: adding additional visual information does not decrease acceptability of the labelling policy compared to a text description.

This is in line with other evidence for food policy research, which finds that communicating evidence via different modalities (visualising versus re-expressing) leads to similar levels of public support and perceived effectiveness (Reyolds et al., 2022).

text.text: Given that imagery may have other wider benefits such as increasing understanding of a policy, this has important implications for policy communication.

However, this finding needs to be replicated for other labelling types, as previous studies measuring the acceptability of health warnings have focused on graphic HWLs that contain an image alongside a text warning, whereas the current study used textonly HWLs.

These warnings were selected as they are most likely to be introduced as a policy, but future research should also investigate any differences in acceptability for less accepted policies such as graphic HWLs, which have been shown to be less accepted in general and evoke stronger reactions -such as negative emotions -compared to text-only HWLs (Clarke et al., 2021).

text.text: In terms of secondary outcomes, there were no differences in the perceived effectiveness of the labels at changing the participant's behaviour or the public's behaviour by either label type or between describing versus visualising the labelling policy.

Based on overall scores that agreed to some extent with labels being effective in reducing drinking, participants did not view the labels as being particularly effective in getting them to drink less (36-44%) but were more likely to say they were useful in getting others to drink less (59-65%).

In the freetext comments, half of the participants thought the labels might have some benefits on reducing drinking at a population level and 17% of participants highlighted they may be effective for specific groups, such as heavy drinkers.
This is in line with evidence that the public often believe policies are more effective for other than themselves (Cornwell & Krantz, 2014).

text.text: Additionally, the majority of participants in the study were low risk drinkers who may not perceive their drinking as needing to change, and evidence suggests that heavier drinkers are more likely to say they will change drinking patterns in response to calorie labelling than low-risk drinkers (Steptoe et al., 2024).

text.text: In the free-text comments, many of the participants highlighted that the labels could have a beneficial impact on increasing awareness or knowledge, which is in line with previous research suggesting labels may influence these cognitive factors (Correia et al., 2024; Steptoe et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In the free-text comments, many of the participants highlighted that the labels could have a beneficial impact on increasing awareness or knowledge, which is in line with previous research suggesting labels may influence these cognitive factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Correia et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Steptoe et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These potential impacts are important in their own right but may also serve as precursors to behaviour change.
There were no overall differences in perceived harms by either label type or between describing versus visualising the labelling policy.
There were significant interactions for both perceived harms to self and others.
For perceived harm to self this was due to a significant difference between the calorie labelling only and the combined label in the description plus image conditions.
For perceived harms to others this was due to a difference between calorie labelling only and the combined label in the description only conditions.
We cannot identify any plausible explanation for these specific findings, but this may suggest differences in perceived harms for calorie labels alone compared to when presented alongside HWLs.

Given other research has found a difference in response to different combinations of nutrient information and HWLs (Hobin et al., 2024), future research should therefore investigate any differences in perceived harms by different label combinations.
text.formatted: Given other research has found a difference in response to different combinations of nutrient information and HWLs <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hobin et al., 2024)</ref>, future research should therefore investigate any differences in perceived harms by different label combinations.

text.text: Overall, perceived harms to both self and others were low, with the vast majority of participants suggesting that they disagree to some extent that this policy could lead to any harms.

This is in line with research that suggests despite some concerns that calorie information might have adverse consequences there is limited evidence that this is the case (Raffoul et al., 2026) and it may explain why they are a relatively accepted policy.
text.formatted: This is in line with research that suggests despite some concerns that calorie information might have adverse consequences there is limited evidence that this is the case <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Raffoul et al., 2026)</ref> and it may explain why they are a relatively accepted policy.

text.text: However, several participants did raise concerns in the free-text responses about the potential impact of calorie information on individuals with eating disorders (9% of participants in the calorie labelling only groups), suggesting a perception that such labels may be harmful for specific populations.
Similar concerns have been reported in relation to calorie labelling on food menus (Trompeter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similar concerns have been reported in relation to calorie labelling on food menus <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Trompeter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the potential for unintended harms among vulnerable groups should remain an important focus of future research.
This pre-registered randomised study is the first to our knowledge to directly compare the acceptability of HWLs and calorie information.
The sample was representative of a UK population.
This study has some limitations.
First, as we were primarily interested in the differences in responses to different labels we did not include a control group.

Future studies could therefore investigate attitudes towards labelling policies compared to a control label, for example if they seek to assess differences in responses compared to current information included on alcohol product packaging.
Second, the majority of drinkers in the study were low risk.

Given a potential difference in attitudes towards labelling by drinking level (Steptoe et al., 2024), further evidence is needed to investigate any differences in response to labelling interventions by drinking characteristics.

text.text: Finally, the sample was representative of the UK population but participants were highly educated overall, although there is evidence to suggest that responses to labelling may not differ by SES group (Robinson et al., 2022).

text.text: Health warnings and calorie labels on alcohol Using labels based on those being proposed for implementation in Ireland, we found that overall alcohol HWLs and calorie information are perceived as relatively acceptable, although HWLs were less accepted than calorie labelling.
We found no differences in acceptability when describing an alcohol labelling policy compared to when showing an example image alongside the policy description.

Although further evaluation with other labelling interventions is warranted, this suggests giving the public more detailed and visual information about a labelling policy does not decrease acceptability of the policy.
